Issued at 237 AM CDT Mon Sep 14 2026

COOL MORNING TEMPERATURES...Early morning surface analysis samples 
expansive 1020s mb surface high centered over WI. The influence of 
the high has supported the continuation of Sunday evening's clear 
skies and light winds, which has resulted in a quick drop in 
temperatures. As of 2 AM, several locations across central/eastern 
MN (outside of the TC heat island) and western WI are reporting 
temperatures in the mid 40s. Increasing clouds over southwestern MN 
have worked to slow cooling which is reflected by temperatures in 
the 50s at this hour. The tranquil weather conditions will not 
persist much longer as an incoming weather system will bring 
widespread rain and gusty winds across the Upper Midwest today. 

WIDESPREAD RAIN TODAY...The well-advertised incoming round of rain 
remains on track with no major changes to the anticipated soggy 
start to the workweek. Driving today's precipitation is an upper-low 
that is forecast to deepen as it moves across the International 
Border over the next 24-hours. GOES water vapor imagery captures the 
upper-low currently over NW Montana, along with a region of broad 
ascent moving east of the Rockies into the northern Plains. Ahead of 
the upper-low, a strengthening low-level jet is oriented from south 
to north across the Plains. The jet is supporting the advection of 
anomalous moisture that can be characterized by PWATs of ~1.8" or 
so, which is roughly 200% of normal. Guidance remains in solid 
agreement with the development of a broad precipitation shield 
driven by isentropic ascent that will overspread the forecast area 
as the LLJ axis shifts east this morning. We've leaned on hi-res 
guidance for some minor tweaks to onset times in the grids, so 
expect the first raindrops to fall along the MN River in western MN 
by 8-9 AM, beginning in Mankato between 9-10 AM, reaching St. Cloud 
& the Twin Cities between 11AM-Noon, and Eau Claire around 1-2 PM. A 
few rumbles of thunder are possible. We've followed the dayshift in 
dropping temperatures a few degrees below the NBM to account for 
limited heating due to clouds and precipitation.

Rain chances will begin to decrease by late afternoon/early evening 
across far western MN as the low-level jet shifts east and the upper-
level dry slot wraps across the Dakotas. However, PoPs remain higher 
longer into the evening across eastern MN & western WI given the 
position of the LLJ and the northward advance of a warm front out of 
northern IA. A renewed band of showers & a few storms is most 
likely to extend along and east of a line from Albert Lea to Red 
Wing, as highlighted by the HREF. Surface temperatures will warm this 
evening across southern MN and western WI as the warm front draws 
near. In other words, the true "high temperature" will likely be 
observed shortly before midnight and look to be somewhere in the mid-
60s for many locations (compared the 50s expected during the main 
precipitation window this afternoon). Rain chances end from west to 
east through the late evening. When all is said and done, most 
locations will observe at least a half inch of rainfall. Many 
locations look to make a run towards 1" or so, with the main axis of 
1-1.5" amounts forecast to setup across southeastern MN/western WI 
(largely due to the evening rain/storms discussed previously). In 
addition to the rain, it will be a windy day as strong southeasterly 
winds gust upwards of 30-35 mph.

LOOKING AHEAD...The upper-low and associated surface system will 
move north of the Great Lakes by tomorrow morning. A trailing cold 
front is progged to move southeastward across the forecast area by 
daybreak and will set the stage for a nice Tuesday, owing largely to 
the advection of drier air from the northwest. Precipitation chances 
return Wednesday as a wave within zonal flow aloft supports the 
northward retreat of Tuesday's front. The highest rain chances exist 
across southern MN (60-70%), with PoPs lowering to slight chance (20-
30%) over central MN. The active pattern will send another wave from 
the Plains into the Upper Midwest on Friday and it's looking 
plausible that this may be our next round of beneficial rainfall. 
We're still a few days out from having higher confidence, but it's 
important to note that ensemble systems have trended upwards with 
prospects of 1"+ rainfall in the Friday-early Saturday timeframe. 
NBM has followed this idea with 60-80% PoPs now featured in the 
grids. A potentially stronger upper-low is progged to come ashore in 
the Pacific NW late this week and may spawn additional rain chances 
by the time it reaches the north central CONUS later in the upcoming 
weekend. All of this to say the overall forecast looks active, with 
a few chances of some much needed rain potentially in the cards. 
With multiple precipitation windows and an overall active theme, 
don't see any reason to diverge from NBM's highs in the low 70s for
